To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

parenting is mediated by a complex, distributed, and highly interconnected brain circuitry that is comprised of highly conserved brain networks that support emotion, motivation, attention and decision-making.

the human brain's response to infant stimuli is highly complex, with a variety of brain regions involved in the processing of infant stimuli and that the brain regions activated by infant stimuli are similar in some respects to those activated by adult stimuli that are associated with social bonding.

the brain regions involved in parenting include the amygdala, anterior cingulate cortex, insular cortex, hypothalamus, orbitofrontal cortex, periaqueductal gray, prefrontal cortex, and ventral tegmental area.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the brain basis of early parent-child interactions and the implications of this work for understanding the development of the parent-child relationship.
the neural basis of the human capacity for social attachment and social bonding, which is the basis of human parenting.
the neurobiology of the parent-infant relationship, with the goal of understanding the neural mechanisms that support effective and healthy parenting.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
parenting is a highly complex, multi-faceted, and dynamic behavior that is supported by a highly complex, highly conserved, and highly dynamic set of brain circuits.
the neurobiology of human parenting is a very active area of current research, and that it is likely that the neurobiological underpinnings of parenting are highly conserved across species.
the neurobiology of parental caregiving behavior is an exciting and rapidly developing field that is likely to have profound clinical implications.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the human brain is designed to be social.
the brain circuits that support parenting behavior are similar to those supporting other forms of social behavior, and are highly conserved across mammalian species.
a parent's response to an infant is a function of the parent's brain.
The main takeaway from our work is that
parenting is not a single behavior, but rather a set of complex behaviors that are regulated by highly conserved, but distributed, brain networks that support the many facets of parenting.
parenting is a complex behavior, requiring a complex network of brain regions.
the brain circuitry for parenting is not fixed and immutable but rather is malleable, and thus can be influenced by experience.
